newsitem.title: UK: Sterling falls on British election announcement.
newsitem.headline: Sterling falls on British election announcement.

text.p: The pound tumbled against the mark on Monday as long-awaited news of a date for a British election prompted investors to take profits on long sterling positions, analysts said.

Speculation that May 1 would be the day Prime Minister John Major will call the British electorate to the polls had been rife ahead of the announcement, sending sterling sharply lower against the mark.

Media reports over the weekend that Major would confirm the election date as May 1, long seen as his preferred day, drove sterling down by more than two and a half pfennigs in the first few hours of European trade.
The early plunge left it little room to drop further when Prime Minister John Major emerged from his London residence at midday to tell reporters of the decision.
Following his announcement, the pound stood still for a while before ticking slightly higher.

"There were no surprises at all in the announcement... Basically the uncertainties (regarding politics) are out of the way and it looks like relief in the markets, really," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
Sterling was at 2.6835 marks in European afternoon trading, off its session low of 2.6795 marks which was also a six-week low and against 2.7125 in late trade on Friday.
Analysts were surprised at the extent of sterling's drop, given that market operators had long been aware that May 1 was the favoured date and that the opposition Labour party would most likely win.

The market, they said, had judged it was time for the pound to weaken a bit since it had been doing very well against the mark lately, having hit its highest level since September 1992 earlier this month.

"People have had an excellent run on sterling and I think we can probably now expect some more profit-taking on long sterling positions into the election," said Brian Martin, chief economist of foreign exchange at BZW here.

Evidence of this was the fact that sterling's fall against the dollar was not nearly as extensive as its loss against the mark, they said. The pound was at 1.5910 dollars, down from its late Friday level of 1.6012.
Analysts said the market would focus on the election campaign, though they added it was not likely to yield many radical ideas.

"I think the market is more or less resigned to the fact that whoever wins is going to follow a fairly sensible policy," HSBC's David said, adding that the Labour party's plans on public finances would be an area of major interest.

Labour is well placed to end its 18 years in opposition, with its huge lead of about 25 percentage points over the ruling Conservatives in the opinion polls. Under its leader Tony Blair, the party has moved from the left wing of British politics.
This, however, is making it difficult to discern between the two parties' stance on various issues.

"This election should be a lot less newsy than previous ones because the two parties are much closer in economic policy than they were before," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange economist at Lehman Brothers here.
Breedon said a live televised debate between Major, Blair and perhaps the leaders of other parties, if it materialises, would be a highlight of the campaign.
"A live debate does contain the possibility of upsetting things. You can see it would be quite risky from Blair's point of view, it could become quite difficult for him," he said.
Some pointed out that a campaign of six weeks, the longest in 80 years, could be a negative for sterling in some ways.

"From the foreign investors' perspective, the longer it (the campaign) is, the less favourable a light it will cast on the UK scene, if you've got two parties trading insults for six weeks," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
